To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expansion of HIV services has led to a deterioration of patient experiences in Swaziland due to a lack of human resources and the overburdening of health workers.
task shifting has had a positive impact on the continuum of HIV care in Swaziland and that the impact of task shifting should not be measured only in terms of increased access to HIV services.
task shifting is not the same as task sharing, and that the former is likely to undermine rather than improve patient experiences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quality of care, and the need to shift care, rather than simply shifting tasks.
how to improve the quality of patient care in the context of a health system that is under pressure to expand rapidly.
the quality of the patient experience of care, which is not only a question of health worker-patient relationships but also a question of how health care is organized and delivered.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
task shifting, as it has been conceived of and implemented in Swaziland in recent years, has been a mixed bag of good and bad.

, in the quest to reach universal early access to ART, donors, states and health workers must go beyond the strengthening of health systems, and strive to enhance patient experiences and take health workers’ limitations into consideration.
the task shifting of care and logistical responsibilities to expert clients has been a mixed success in terms of the therapeutic experience of patients and the quality of care they receive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
task shifting is an important strategy for achieving treatment scale-up, but it is not sufficient.
the global HIV strategy is not working in its current form and needs to be revisited.
the task shifting of key care tasks to expert clients is not a sustainable strategy for the long-term.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global HIV treatment strategy has been successful in expanding treatment, but has not adequately considered how this expansion will affect patient experiences and health worker well-being.

the task-shifting of care practices to expert clients should not be seen as a panacea to address health system problems but rather as a way of reconfiguring care practices in ways that may be more effective and sustainable.
the global HIV strategy of task shifting must be reconceptualized as a strategy of shifting care practices, and that the patient’s experience should be at the centre of such a strategy.
